body.text: Simplifying your supermarket shop to make healthier choices doesn't need to be overwhelming.
Here are some evidence-based tips to make it easier to choose nutritious food and avoid marketing spin, informed by dieticians Daisy Coyle and Evangeline Mantzioris.
For a deep dive into food packaging claims — which to believe and which to ignore — head to our interactive story.
Note: This article contains general information only. For personal advice, consult a qualified professional.
The basics
Ensure your trolley includes:
• Vegetables (frozen or tinned is fine)
• Protein (unprocessed meats, fish, eggs, legumes or other products)
• Calcium (dairy products like cheese, milk and yoghurt, or fortified plant-based alternatives)
Limit packaged snack foods and desserts.
Focus your shop on the outside sections of the supermarket (for example, fresh produce and dairy), rather than the packaged or health food aisles.
Check your most-purchased items
You don't have to pore over every product you purchase, but dieticians suggest checking the back of the packaging for the food and drinks you buy habitually.
Most packaged foods must list all ingredients in descending order of weight. The list must also show the percentage of the key ingredients in a food.
When you scan the ingredient list, consider:
• What's the main ingredient? Are you buying what you think you're buying?
• How does the ingredient list align with how the food is marketed?
• How long is the list of ingredients?
• How recognisable are the ingredients?

If the key ingredient is lower than you'd expect (for example, tinned tomatoes containing only 60 per cent tomato), the product may be bulked out with additives or concentrates, which are less nutritious.
If the list is long and the ingredients hard to understand, the product is likely an ultra-processed food (UPF), which health experts say we should try to limit where possible.
Review the nutrition panel
Focus on the per 100 grams column, not the serving size, which is decided by the food company.
Compare what you see with the following recommendations from the National Health and Medical Research Council.
10g or less per 100g or 100mL
Exceptions: 2g or less for milk, yoghurt and ice-cream, 15g or less for cheese
If more, check that sugar (or alternative names for added sugar - see below) is not listed high on the ingredient list
Alternative names for sugar include sucrose, glucose, maltose dextrose, high fructose corn syrup, corn syrup, rice syrup, maple syrup, invert sugar and fruit juice concentrate.
You can find more information in the Australian dietary guidelines.
Look for a Health Star Rating
The Health Star Rating is a government-led labelling system that rates the overall nutrition of a product from 0.5 stars to five.
• Use the Health Star Rating to compare products in the same category, rather than comparing foods in different categories.
• Because the system is currently voluntary, research shows that food companies tend to leave off the rating if it's low.
• A rating can be a useful guide, but it won't tell the whole story (for example, it won't tell you whether a product is ultra-processed). For that, check the ingredient list.
If you want to dive deeper, you can also use the Health Star Rating calculator to assess foods and drinks.
Scan for the spin
Take a moment to think about the product you're considering. What claims are on the front? What pictures or designs catch your eye?
• What drew me to this product?
• What is the marketing telling me?
• How much do the ingredients and nutrition panel align with the marketing messages?
Remember: words like "natural", "pure", "organic" and "healthy" are marketing terms and don't necessarily mean a product is good for you.
In kids' foods — some of the most heavily marketed foods around — this often includes phrases like "no nasties", "happy tummies" or "kid-approved".

Other terms, like "source of fibre", "low-fat" or "no added sugar", must be based in fact but can also be misleading. (For example, a product can have no added sugar but still be high in naturally occurring sugars.)
Eat what you love
Dr Mantzioris says "you should never beat yourself up over what you choose to eat".
She suggests
• Taking a big-picture view of your diet. Focus on what you eat regularly, rather than special occasions.
• Making small changes that feel achievable and not punitive. (For example, choose water over soft drink sometimes, or swap out processed meat in your lunch sandwich.)
• If you decide to have a treat, enjoy it!
"If you feel like chocolate and you do buy it, make sure you enjoy it. Buy the best quality you can and don't feel guilty while you're consuming it," Dr Mantzioris says.
"Dietitians and nutritionists don't really care what you have on Christmas or birthdays. It's not the occasional things that impact on your diet, it's what you do every day.
"The more vegetables or legumes you can get in, whatever you're choosing, the better."
